components.html:
Welcome, {First}!
This cute-as-a-button baby set is from a vintage magazine. Knit it Now has converted the pattern to our dynamic format, allowing you to use any yarn, any stitch pattern and any gauge machine.
This course is designed to walk you though knitting the sweater, leggings and blanket and offers options for making the set your own. It is an opportunity for you to gain confidence in your knitting.
A little planning can go a long way!
  • Have you ever started a project unsure of the techniques needed to finish it?
  • Want to create something that you will be proud of... good enough to give as a gift?
This course will walk you through all the planning steps. It shows techniques that may be new to you and helps you record your progress. As you knit, you can refer to the videos as often as you like. Work the practice swatches and following the actual pattern will be a breeze!
If this is your first machine knitted project or your tenth, follow along, the skills you gain here will be invaluable for future knitting projects .. not just knitting for baby!
If you are new here, the next lesson will help you learn to navigate this course so you can get the most benefit from the material that is included. Help is as close as the help icon above.

The video will walk you through how to access the lessons and navigate to get the most out of your course.
Don't skip lessons ... you may feel that you know about a certain technique ... but sometimes you will pick up a new tip that you can use while watching a video.
Another reason to follow the course material in order - Throughout the lessons, you'll be making decisions about your project.  We will record your decisions to create your Custom Pattern and your Course Binder that you can download to refer back to again and again.

For the original design, the leggings and the sweater are knit at different gauges.
It is critical that you swatch for ALL the stitch patterns you will be using.
  • In the image below, the top example shows 80 stitches knit at 7 stitches per inch. The finished size is a bit over 11"
  • The lower example is 80 stitches knit at 8 stitches per inch in pattern. The difference is over an inch!
If you build your pattern and generate your knitting instructions at the same gauge, your knitted pieces will not be correct. (think ... poorly fitting sweaters here)
The same holds true for the row gauge. The original sweater was knit in tuck.
  • On the left shows 50 rows knit at 16 rows per inch
  • On the right is 50 rows knit at 10 rows per inch. Almost 2" difference in this small sample

Your Turn: Examine the differences between stitch patterns
If you don't know the answers below, guess ... we'll show you the math.
The pattern instructs us to cast on 80 stitches.

A common alternative to shaping a neckline while knitting in pattern is to use cut 'n sew. (Actually many knitters use cut 'n sew exclusively.)
Even if you are a "purist" and feel that you MUST shape a neckline, we encourage you to try the cut 'n sew exercise for practice.
Once you get over the fear of cutting your knitting, you may become a convert to the technique.
Template for Cut 'n Sew Neckline for this pattern.

Use an existing swatch or knit a swatch approx 8" x 8". This will mimic knitting the front of your sweater with no neck shaping.
If you've never cut your knitting, take a deep breath and cut away! You'll be surprised how stable most knitting is. Careful sewing and handling will ensure that the stitches don't run.
  1. Block your swatch to tame any curling edges and set the stitches.
  2. Mark a curved neckline along the bind off edge of the swatch. Use a fabric marker, pencil or marker (this will be covered by your band)
  3. Using a sewing machine or serger, stitch along the marked line, securing the knitting. Stitch multiple times if needed to make sure the stitches are secure.
  4. Cut along the inside of the sewing
  5. Don't like the shape? Go ahead and re-stitch till you get it right
Use the template provided in this course, the Knit it Now Templates in our store, a plate, cup, or bowl ... anything to get a nice looking neckline opening.

This neck opening has a bit of an unusual shape. Because the sweater a pullover, we are unable to pick up stitches around the neck opening and knit a band in one piece (as we would a cardigan).
Whether you shaped your neckline or used Cut 'n Sew here's a neat method of knitting and attaching the neckband.

NOTE: It's always best to measure and double check the stitch count for the band in any pattern.
  1. Knit the front and back
  2. Join the shoulders
  3. Measure your neck opening and multiply that measurement by your band stitch gauge
  4. Reduce the stitch count by approx 10%
  5. Use a closed cast on method and knit the first half of your band at a slightly tighter tension than your garment tension.
  6. Knit a turning row
  7. Knit the second half of the band
  8. Scrap Off
  9. Sandwich the cut edge of the garment between the 2 halves of the band and neatly stitch the band in place.
TIP: Attach the inside of the band first, then neatly backstitch through the live stitches (on scrap) for a beautiful finish.

slides.caption: Front neck is ready for cut 'n sew. Notice the waste yarn on the back
Sewing machine or serger. Be sure to secure the stitches.
Join the shoulders. Notice the back neck is not joined.
Cut and  joined and ready for the neckband.
This neckline can't be attached by machine.  We'll need to measure, calculate, knit the band separately and attach it by hand.

• Fold the sweater in half and measure the neckline opening
  • Multiply the total neck opening times the band stitch gauge
  • Reduce by 10%
  • The result is the number of band stitches to cast on

• Ewrap cast on
  • Knit the first half of the band
  • Knit a turning row
  • Knit the second half of the band
The waste yarn edge is folded to the public side.
Neatly stitch the e-wrap edge to the inside of the neck opening.
Neatly backstitch the live stitches in place on the public side of the neck opening.
The finished neck band ... ready to work the back neck opening.

components.html:
Use the neckline shaping swatch you knit previously and add a neckband following the examples in the video from the previous lesson.
DON'T SKIP THIS STEP
You are taking this course to improve your knitting skills. Whether you use cut 'n sew, or shape your necklines, please try AT LEAST 1 band method before starting your project sweater.
Adding neckbands can be one of the more challenging part of knitting sweaters.
There are so many variables: Stitch patterns, garment size, yarn types, techniques ... take time to discover a method that works for you, so there will be no panic when it comes time to finish your project sweater.

Practice Suggestions

  1. Shape a neckline
    - With the public side of the neckline facing, rehang the neck opening on the machine
    - Knit a band and loosely bind off
    - Fold the band to the private side of the neckline and stitch in place
  2. Shape or cut 'n sew a neckline
    - With the private side of the neckline facing, rehang the neck opening on the machine
    - Create a band ending with scrap yarn.
    - Fold the scrap edge to the public side of the sweater
    - Neatly backstitch the live stitches in place and remove the scrap
  3. Shape or cut 'n sew a neckline and add a "sandwiched band" as shown in the button band lesson in this course.
  4. Shape a neckline and work a row of single crochet, then a decorative crochet edge. You may be surprised at how quickly this works up and what a beautiful addition it will be to your sweater (especially for girls)
    5. Although this infant sweater neckline is small and can't be hung directly on the machine, the following video gives an excellent overview of necklines. While you are practicing, try the techniques presented. You'll apply them again and again in your knitting.

These little bands are a perfect opportunity to try a new band technique.
Watch as we create a "sandwiched" band that is beautiful on both the inside and the outside.

Adding buttonholes shouldn't be intimidating. The following video shows a number of different buttonhole techniques. For this small sweater, one or two stitch eyelet will probably be your best bet.
You'll work the buttonhole on both sides of the button band. When the band is complete, stitch around each buttonhole to join them together.

Before starting your sweater: Using the edge of a swatch, practice creating a 2 piece band.
As you are working the band, try working 2 stitch eyelet buttonholes.
Instructions are for standard gauge (mid/bulky gauge) machines.
2 Stitch Eyelet Buttonhole Practice
  1. Cast on 40 (20) stitches with any method
  2. Knit for 16 (8) rows
  3. Identify your buttonhole placement and mark your needlebed
  4. Buttonhole Row 1: Transfer one stitch left and one stitch right
  5. Leave emptied needles in out of work position
  6. Knit across
  7. Pick up the loose loop and hang it on one of the buttonhole needles. Put this needle in working position
  8. Knit across
  9. Pick up the loose strand from the previous row and hang it on the emptied needle. Put this needle in working position
  10. Knit for 16 (8) rows
  11. Repeat the buttonhole rows for the second side of the band
  12. Knit for 16 (8) rows
  13. Bind off
  14. Fold the sample band in half, line up the buttonholes and neatly stitch around each buttonhole to secure them together

Knit the sleeves from the top down or the bottom up ... it's your choice.
Knit them in the same yarn and stitch pattern as the body ... or mix it up!
However you choose to knit your sleeves, use the same ribbed cuff techniques as the leggings cuffs.

NOTE: If your gauge is different for the different pieces in this project, change your gauge information here and "Generate your Pattern" multiple times. Don't forget that you don't have to print the entire pattern each time. Use your PDF reader to print only the pages you want.

components.html:
TOP DOWN
  • Cast on and hang a hem for the waistband elastic
  • Knit the body of the leggings and each leg separately
  • Complete the cuffs ... (lots of options here)
CUFF UP
  • Cast on and knit a cuff
  • Knit the first leg and remove the knitting on waste yarn (or garter bar)
  • Cast on and knit the second cuff and leg
  • Rehang the first leg and add stitches in the crotch area (cast on instead of binding off the crotch stitches)
  • Knit the body of the leggings
  • Create a casing for elastic by working a Reverse Hung Hem

Top Down Option:
Hang a hem to form a casing for the waistband. 2 versions are offered in the video. Which do you prefer?

Cuff Up Option
When knitting from the cuff up a reverse hung hem is needed to form the casing.

Less Bulk Option
For a much neater waistband, use mock ribbing to create the casing.

The blanket in the original project is knit in the tuck stitch pattern included with the pattern. To neatly finish the edges, a binding was created in the same tuck stitch pattern alternating 3 colors.

You can choose to knit your blanket in any stitch pattern, but the binding technique is priceless! So many knitters struggle with curled and/or unfinished edges on blankets. Although not a beginner technique, it is one you should consider for your knitting.
The following video explores some options for creating a binding for your blanket.
You'll need to understand short row increases and short row decreases. The next lesson includes instruction and practice for these techniques.

Practice before knitting the binding for your blanket
  • Establish how wide you want to your binding
  • Play with stitch patterns and color
  • Experiment with sew-as-you-go verses an independent binding
  • Master mitered corners
Follow the video in the previous lesson.
Instructions are for standard gauge (mid/bulky gauge) machines.
  • Cast on 31(17) stitches
  • Knit even for 3-4"
  • Set your carriage to hold
  • *On the carriage side pull one end needle to hold position - KNIT ACROSS*
  • Repeat from * to * until 3 needles are in working position
  • *On the carriage side push one middle needle to working position- KNIT ACROSS*
  • Repeat from * to * until all needles are in working position
  • Knit 3" - 4"
  • Bind off

components.html:
Joining a panel of knitting to another panel as you knit, makes for fast finishing. Using this technique will speed up the finishing of the blanket binding for this project.
If you've never tried sew-as-you-go, we recommend you take this opportunity to try it along the edge of a swatch. This is a technique that you will use again and again in your knitting... not just for blankets.

Ribbed cuffs on the leggings help keep the pants in place (and little legs warm). Ribbed cuffs on the sweater add a nice touch as well.
No matter what direction you are knitting the leggings or the sleeves, one option is to put the cuff stitches on waste yarn. Finish the knitting and seam the front and back pieces of the leggings (or the underarm seam of the sleeve). Then pick up the live stitches from waste yarn on hand knitting needles and hand knit the ribbing the ribbing in the round (no seams).

On the machine, you have many options for cuffs:

Top Down
  1. As you finish each leg or sleeve, transfer every other stitch to the ribber and knit ribbing. You'll need to insert a cast on comb to successfully knit the ribbing. See the video below.
  2. Cast on and knit your ribbed cuffs first, removing them on waste yarn. When both the front and back leggings pieces (or the sleeves) are finished and the cuffs are scrapped off, join the seams. Rehang the ribbing on the main bed, rehang the cuff edge on the same needles and loosely bind off.
Cuff Up
  1. Start your leg or sleeves pieces with ribbing and knit up to the waist or shoulder.
  2. Start your leg or sleeves pieces with mock ribbing and knit up to the waist or shoulder.
  3. Start your leggings or sleeves with scrap yarn and attach a pre-knit ribbed cuff as above.

You have knitting on the main bed and you want to switch to ribbing. It's critical to have even weight on the work for the ribbing to knit properly.
  • Transfer the stitches to the ribber in the needle arrangement of your choice, then insert the ribber cast on comb as normal
~~~~ or ~~~~
  • Scrap off the knitting, hang the ribber cast on comb in some scrap knitting and ravel cord. Rehang the knitting, transfer the stitches and knit your ribbing.
